summary: Specifies the OpenPGP message formats, which provide public key and symmetric encryption, digital signatures, compression, and key management. It exists so developers can build interoperable applications and is not a step-by-step cookbook. It obsoletes RFC 4880, RFC 5581, and RFC 6637.

plainLanguage.summary: OpenPGP defines how keys, signatures and encrypted messages are written down, so that different programs can read each other's files. It covers public key encryption, digital signatures, compression and key management. RFC 9580 is the current version of those formats, and it replaces three earlier RFCs.

questions: what is the difference between v4 and v6 openpgp keys
subtitle: The message, key and signature formats behind PGP-style encryption, now with version 6 keys, modern curves and authenticated encryption.

tldr.problem: Programs need one agreed way to encrypt data, sign it, and exchange the public keys and certificates that make both work, so that one implementation can read another's output.
tldr.mechanism: OpenPGP defines a stream of typed packets: session keys encrypted to each recipient's public key, an encrypted data container, signatures, and key packets bound together by self-signatures. ASCII Armor wraps the binary stream in printable text.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9580 is the current revision. It obsoletes RFC 4880, RFC 5581 and RFC 6637, adds version 6 keys and signatures, X25519 and Ed25519, AEAD encryption and Argon2, and deprecates RSA, DSA, ElGamal, MD5 and SHA-1.

today: RFC 9580 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2024. It obsoletes RFC 4880, RFC 5581 and RFC 6637, and no RFC obsoletes or updates it. The document itself lists the algorithms that must now be supported, the older ones that must no longer be used, and test vectors for implementers in its appendices.

sections.title: What OpenPGP Specifies
sections.content:
RFC 9580 specifies the message formats used in OpenPGP. OpenPGP provides encryption with public key or symmetric algorithms, digital signatures, compression and key management. The document is maintained so that developers can build applications that work with each other.

It is a revision of RFC 4880, which revised RFC 2440, which replaced RFC 1991. This document also obsoletes RFC 5581, which added the Camellia cipher to OpenPGP, and RFC 6637, which added elliptic curves to OpenPGP. It carries all outstanding verified errata from those documents, and Appendix B lists what changed for implementers.

The document is clear about its own limits. It is not a step-by-step guide for writing an application, and it does not cover storage and implementation questions. It does discuss the implementation details needed to avoid security flaws.

An implementation MAY support compression, and SHOULD support base64 conversion. A signature-only implementation is reasonable: it is non-conformant only in that it omits encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: OpenPGP is a set of file formats for keys, signatures and encrypted messages, so that different programs can read each other's output. RFC 9580 is the current version of those formats. It replaces three earlier RFCs and tells implementers exactly what the bytes must look like, without telling them how to build an application around it.

sections.title: Encryption and Signatures Step by Step
sections.content:
Confidentiality and authentication are separate services, and a message may use either one or both.

For encryption, the sender generates a random session key for the message and uses it only once. The session key is encrypted with each recipient's public key, and those encrypted session keys start the message. The message itself is encrypted with a message key derived from the session key, after optional compression. The recipient decrypts the session key with their private key, then decrypts the message and decompresses it if needed. When a passphrase is used instead of a public key, the passphrase is converted into a key in a similar way.

For a digital signature, the sender computes a hash digest of the message and signs that digest with the sender's private key. The signature travels with the message or beside it. The receiver hashes the received message again and verifies it against the signature. A successful verification means the message is authentic.

To use both services on one message, the sender signs the message first, then encrypts the message and its signature together, and finally encrypts the session key to each recipient.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message gets a fresh random key. That key is locked separately for every recipient, and the message is locked with it once. A signature works the other way: the sender hashes the message and signs the hash, so the reader can check that the message has not changed.

sections.title: Packets, Headers and Criticality
sections.content:
An OpenPGP message, keyring, certificate or detached signature is a sequence of packets. Each packet has a header carrying a Type ID and the length, followed by a body. That length is the canonical source of packet boundaries: a parser MUST find the next packet at the exact offset the header gives and MUST NOT read octets outside that range.

There are two header formats. The current OpenPGP format sets bits 7 and 6 of the first octet to one and carries the Type ID in bits 5 to 0, so it can encode IDs up to 63. The Legacy format, used by implementations that predate any IETF specification of OpenPGP, leaves bit 6 zero and has only four bits for the Type ID, so it can encode IDs below 16. Legacy packets MAY be read but SHOULD NOT be generated, and that format was obsoleted by RFC 2440 in 1998.

Lengths come in four forms. One octet covers up to 191 octets, two octets cover 192 to 8383, five octets cover up to 4,294,967,295, and Partial Body Length headers are powers of two from 1 to 1,073,741,824, which turn a packet into a stream of parts. Partial lengths may only be used for literal, compressed or encrypted data packets, and the first one MUST be at least 512 octets.

Packet criticality is how the format stays open to change. Type IDs from 0 to 39 are critical, so an unknown critical packet means the whole packet sequence MUST be rejected. Type IDs from 40 to 63 are non-critical, and an unknown one MUST be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything in OpenPGP is wrapped in a labelled envelope that says what it is and how long it is. An envelope marked as important has to be understood, or the whole file is refused. An envelope marked as optional can be skipped. That rule is how new features get added without breaking older software.

sections.title: Signature Types and Subpackets
sections.content:
A Signature packet binds a public key to some data. The most common ones are a signature over a document and a certification of a User ID. Version 3 signatures carry only basic information. Versions 4 and 6 add subpackets, small extension records that hold extra information about the signature or the key.

A version 4 or version 6 signature holds two sets of subpackets. The hashed area is covered by the signature itself. The unhashed area has no cryptographic protection and is advisory only. An implementation MUST generate a version 6 signature when signing with a version 6 key and a version 4 signature when signing with a version 4 key, and MUST NOT create version 3 signatures.

The signature type says what the signature is for. Types 0x00 and 0x01 sign a document, 0x02 signs only the subpackets of the signature itself, 0x10 to 0x13 certify that a User ID and a public key belong together, 0x18 binds a subkey to its primary key, 0x19 is the reverse statement made by the subkey, 0x1F attaches information straight to a key, 0x20 and 0x28 revoke a key or a subkey, 0x30 revokes a certification, 0x40 is a timestamp and 0x50 confirms somebody else's signature. The RFC calls the vagueness of the certification types a feature, because the receiver has final authority over validity. Most implementations issue generic certifications, type 0x10.

Version 6 signatures add a random salt that is hashed before any other data. Its size follows the hash algorithm: 16 octets for SHA2-256, 24 for SHA2-384 and 32 for SHA2-512. Because the salt is new every time, signing the same message twice produces two different signatures.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature says what it is for. It can show that a document is unchanged, that a name belongs to a key, that a spare key belongs to a main key, or that a key has been withdrawn. Version 6 signatures add random data to the mix, so signing the same file twice gives two different results.

sections.title: Key Packets, Fingerprints and Key IDs
sections.content:
Key material comes in four packet variants: Public Key, Public Subkey, Secret Key and Secret Subkey, and each variant comes in four versions. Versions 2 and 3 have been deprecated since 1998, version 4 is deprecated by this document, and version 6 is current. Implementations SHOULD create keys with version 6 format, SHOULD NOT generate version 4 or version 3 keys, and SHOULD accept both.

Every key has a fingerprint and a Key ID. The Key ID is always 64 bits; the fingerprint length depends on the version. A version 4 fingerprint is the 160-bit SHA-1 hash of the octet 0x99, the 2-octet packet length and the whole Public Key packet, and its Key ID is the low 64 bits of that fingerprint. A version 6 fingerprint is the 256-bit SHA2-256 hash of the octet 0x9B, the 4-octet packet length and the Public Key packet, and its Key ID is the first 64 bits. Implementations SHOULD NOT assume that Key IDs are unique, and the RFC notes that two different keys can share one.

A version 6 public key packet adds a 4-octet count of the public key material, which helps a parser cope with an unknown algorithm. A secret key packet appends the secret material to the public fields. Its first octet says how the secret material is protected: zero for unprotected, 253 for AEAD, 254 for CFB and 255 for the deprecated MalleableCFB. Where a passphrase protects the key, the passphrase is converted to a key by a string-to-key specifier, and Argon2 is the recommended one because it is memory hard.
sections.plainLanguage: Every OpenPGP key carries a short number that identifies it and a longer hash that is much harder to fake. Version 6 keys use a 256-bit hash; older version 4 keys use a 160-bit one. The short number is not guaranteed to be unique, so it should not be trusted on its own.

sections.title: ASCII Armor and Cleartext Signatures
sections.content:
The underlying representation of OpenPGP objects is a stream of arbitrary octets. Because some systems only accept printable text, the format defines a printable encoding called ASCII Armor: base64 as described in RFC 4648, wrapped into lines of no more than 76 characters. Implementations SHOULD support base64 conversions, and when decoding they MUST ignore all whitespace.

Armor adds a header line, optional headers, a blank line, the data and a tail line. The header line says what is inside: BEGIN PGP MESSAGE for signed, encrypted or compressed files, BEGIN PGP PUBLIC KEY BLOCK, BEGIN PGP PRIVATE KEY BLOCK and BEGIN PGP SIGNATURE. The tail line repeats the text with BEGIN replaced by END. The optional headers are key and value pairs named Version, Comment, Hash and Charset.

An optional 24-bit checksum may follow the base64 data. An implementation MUST NOT reject an object because that footer is missing, malformed or wrong, and it SHOULD NOT be generated, because computing it costs time and adds no meaningful integrity protection. An armored encrypted message that ends in a version 2 encrypted data packet, an armored sequence of version 6 signatures, and an armored version 6 key or keyring MUST NOT carry the footer.

The Cleartext Signature Framework signs readable text without armoring the text itself. The text sits after -----BEGIN PGP SIGNED MESSAGE----- and before an armored signature, and it is dash-escaped so that it cannot be mistaken for armor headers. Trailing spaces and tabs are removed before signing, and the digest is computed over the text rather than over the dash-escaped form.

The RFC is candid about the limits of that framework. It cannot round-trip text where whitespace matters, such as a Unified Diff, and a very large signed text is hard for a person to read and cannot be processed in a single pass. For those cases the RFC recommends a signed message or a detached signature instead.
sections.plainLanguage: OpenPGP data is binary, so it can be wrapped in printable text that survives email and other text-only channels. The wrapper carries a few header lines and a checksum that is now optional and discouraged. A second format signs readable text where it stands, but it strips trailing spaces, so it should not be used for files where spacing matters.

sections.title: Algorithms, AEAD and Deprecated Choices
sections.content:
The registries in this section fix the algorithm IDs that programs use, and each list names a few algorithms that every implementation must support, so that two implementations can always find common ground.

For public key algorithms, implementations MUST implement Ed25519 (27) for signatures and X25519 (25) for encryption, and SHOULD implement Ed448 (28) and X448 (26). For symmetric ciphers, AES-128 MUST be implemented and AES-256 SHOULD be. For hashes, SHA2-256 MUST be implemented and SHA2-384 and SHA2-512 SHOULD be. For AEAD modes, OCB MUST be implemented, while EAX and GCM MAY be. For compression, uncompressed data MUST be implemented, ZLIB SHOULD be, and ZIP should be supported for reading.

Version 2 of the encrypted data container uses authenticated encryption. The packet carries a cipher algorithm ID, an AEAD mode ID, a chunk size octet, 32 octets of salt, the encrypted data and a final authentication tag. The message key is derived from the session key and the salt with HKDF using SHA2-256, giving M + N - 64 bits, where M is the cipher key size and N the nonce size. The data is split into chunks, each chunk gets its own authentication tag, and a final tag covers the empty string plus the total plaintext length, which detects a truncated message. The chunk size octet gives 1 << (c + 6) octets; an implementation MUST accept values from 0 to 16 and MUST NOT create a value larger than 16, which would be 4 MiB chunks.

The older version 1 container is still read but no longer written. It encrypts in CFB mode and appends a 20-octet SHA-1 digest, called the Modification Detection Code, over the prefix data and the plaintext. The RFC notes that authenticated encryption has replaced it.

A long list of older choices is deprecated. RSA (1) keys are deprecated and SHOULD NOT be generated, and no RSA key smaller than 3072 bits may be generated. DSA (17) and Elgamal (16) keys MUST NOT be generated. Signatures MUST NOT be generated with MD5, SHA-1 or RIPEMD-160. Data MUST NOT be encrypted with IDEA, TripleDES or CAST5. Passphrase protection MUST NOT use the Simple string-to-key specifier, and Argon2 is the recommended one.
sections.plainLanguage: The document fixes which algorithms every program must support, so two implementations can always find one they share. It also rules out the old ones. RSA keys are deprecated, DSA and ElGamal keys may no longer be generated, and the IDEA, TripleDES and CAST5 ciphers must no longer be used for new data. The current encrypted container uses authenticated encryption, which detects any change to the data.

sections.title: Certificates and Transferable Keys
sections.content:
A Transferable Public Key, also called a certificate, is what travels between users. The Public Key packet comes first, and the primary key MUST be able to make signatures, because it creates the self-signatures that hold the certificate together. The subkeys may be of any type.

Next come the User ID packets, each one a UTF-8 name and email address for the key owner, each followed by zero or more certification signatures. A certification is the statement that a public key belongs to the person named in that User ID. Other users add certifications of their own, so a key collects several opinions about who owns it.

Then come the subkeys, each followed by a Subkey Binding signature made by the primary key, saying that the primary key owns it. A subkey that can sign must also carry an embedded Primary Key Binding signature, type 0x19, made by the subkey itself. The RFC calls it good practice to use a separate subkey for every job, such as one subkey for signing and another for encryption.

A version 6 certificate has a fixed shape: the primary key, any revocation signatures, a Direct Key signature, then the User ID and User Attribute packets with their certifications, then the subkeys with their binding signatures, and optionally a trailing Padding packet. The Direct Key signature carries the key flags, the expiry and the algorithm preferences. An implementation MUST ensure that a valid Direct Key signature is present before it uses a version 6 key, because that stops an attacker stripping a self-signature that holds an expiry date or a preference. User IDs are explicitly optional in version 6, and a version 6 revocation certificate must include the primary key packet, so that it can be checked on its own.
sections.plainLanguage: A certificate is a public key plus the names attached to it and the signatures that vouch for those names. The main key signs everything else, so it must be a signing key. Separate subkeys do the encryption and signing jobs, and the main key signs a statement tying each one to it.

sections.title: Message Structure and Version Pairing
sections.content:
OpenPGP defines three kinds of packet sequence. A Transferable Public Key is the certificate described above, a Transferable Secret Key is the same thing with the secret parts filled in, and an OpenPGP Message is what an application sends. A message is one of four things: an encrypted message, a signed message, a compressed message or a literal message.

An encrypted message is a sequence of encrypted session key packets followed by one encrypted data packet, and the versions have to line up. A version 1 encrypted data packet must be preceded by version 4 symmetric session key packets and version 3 public session key packets. A version 2 encrypted data packet must be preceded by version 6 packets of both kinds. An implementation processing a message MUST discard any session key packet whose version does not match the payload.

Signature versions line up with key versions in the same way. A version 6 key produces a version 6 signature and a version 6 one-pass signature packet. A version 4 key produces a version 4 signature, but its one-pass signature packet is version 3, because no version 4 of that packet exists. A version mismatch does not invalidate the whole sequence; it invalidates that one signature, which is then ignored for validation.

A detached signature is one or more signature packets stored away from the data they sign, the way a program bundle may carry a file with a signature of that file beside it.
sections.plainLanguage: The document spells out which packets may sit in which order. The rule to remember is that the versions must agree: the packets that unlock a message and the packet that holds the encrypted data are either both old or both new. When they do not agree, the reader drops the ones that do not fit and carries on.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security section covers the attacks the format is built to resist, the mistakes an implementation can make, and the limits of each defence.

MD5 and SHA-1 have known weaknesses, and both are deprecated. SHA-1 cannot be removed entirely, because version 4 key fingerprints are computed with it. An implementation MAY look for the signs of a known SHA-1 collision attack and reject such input, which turns an uncertain failure into an explicit one.

Ciphertext malleability is the problem the newer containers answer. If an attacker can change the ciphertext and it still decrypts to something, the scheme is malleable. The deprecated Symmetrically Encrypted Data packet is malleable, the version 1 container offers only some protection through its SHA-1 digest, and the version 2 container uses authenticated encryption, which detects the change. When the integrity check fails, the implementation MUST NOT release any decrypted data to the user and MUST halt with an error. The RFC states that the old packet MUST NOT be generated and that users are RECOMMENDED to migrate to authenticated encryption.

Two oracles deserve care. The quick check in the older containers, a repeated pair of octets that reveals a wrong passphrase, can be used as an oracle if an automated service answers it quickly enough. Padding errors in PKCS#1 can leak the session key, so implementations SHOULD report one error for every failure and SHOULD use constant-time checks.

The remaining points concern the rest of the system. Random data must come from a cryptographically secure generator. A Padding packet of random octets can hide the length of a message from an observer. The Intended Recipient Fingerprint subpacket stops a signature being forwarded to someone it was not meant for. An implementation SHOULD limit how many layers of compression it will decompress, because a compressed message can expand into itself and exhaust memory. And because a 256-bit version 6 fingerprint is harder for a person to compare than a 160-bit version 4 one, the RFC says to prefer mechanical comparison over manual comparison.
sections.plainLanguage: The security notes explain what can go wrong and what the format does about it. The biggest old problem was that an attacker could change an encrypted message and still have it decrypt. The current container prevents that by checking the data as it is decrypted, and a failed check must stop the program before any text is shown. The notes also cover password guessing, oracles that leak information, and hiding the size of a message.
